sorry, I think there may have been a misunderstanding.

What I meant was a 4th dimension where a point exists as a sphere, whose coordinates would be defined as (x,y,z,r) x,y, and z being the normal three dimensions of a cartesian plane, r being an additional radius.

I agree, it's not a very good example.

a better one would be to have a 4th dimension as the coordinate for the possible set of 3 dimension. i.e. a point with coordinates x,y,z could be an infinite number of points, as the same point exists in an infinite number of 4th dimensions. point x,y,z,d would only be one point, as it would only exist in single fourth, third, second, and first dimension.

#191760 67 2006-06-19T23:24:29Z Topolord
Bob James Samuels was a normal man, he lived in a suburban home outside Chicago, he had a wife, and three kids. His life seemed great, many would say he had everything he ever wanted. But then, on one seemingly average day, Bob cracked.

Co-worker Anthony Squire still recalls that late June moring, "I came into work late that day, and I remember sitting down at my desk hurredly. Bob was at his desk as normal; He didn't look over as I arrived. At about ten o'clock that morning, I got up to get a cup of coffee. When I returned I saw Bob, standing in the middle of the room, blood covering his face, the broken screen of his computer still clutched in his shaking hands. Oh god! I'll never forget the sight of my dead colleagues, my friends..."

After witnessing the horrific scene of carnage described above, Mr. Squire ran to a safe place and notified the police. They were able to catch the deranged Mr. Samuels before he fled the city.

What made Bob Samuels suddenly lose control. He had no history of mental illness, he had a family which loved him. Thanks to the miracle of modern science, the truth behind this shocking tale have now been revealed.

Psycologist Dr. W.P. Swanson, who has worked with Mr. Samuels, has long believed that the sudden insanity of Mr. Samuels stemmed from a deep seated child-hood fear, one of weaponry and its violent effects. This came, Dr. Swanson believes, from an event during Samuels' childhood when he witnessed the brutal murder of his uncle near his apartment in Chicago. Dr. Swanson believes that the way in which Bob replayed the event in his mind cuased an unconcious conection between primal violence and revenge, and the vision of repeated violent death. Now, through the most high-tech methods, his hypothesis is being proven.

A group of scientists at the university of Chicago have analayzed the remains of Mr. Samuels computers, and have managed, with the help of some complex machinery, to find the trigger which set off Bob's sudden and violent attack. "With this new evidence, we have been able to isolate the trigger," One of the researches told me. "The exact cuase of Bob's fit, which unlocked the primal gateway between revenge and his childhood truama, was nothing other than a game. Yes, we have found that Bob was at the time of his attack, playing a simple computer game known as N-game, an addictive free puzzle game. The images of his characters repeated and violent deaths at the hands of guass turrets, rockets, and lasers brought to the surface long lost memories of violence and pain."

All this shows is the importance of psycotherapy, and how important it is to allow your heals to wound. Please, don't bottle up your emotions, let them out early, and then live your life. To conclude, I will share with you a usefull piece of advice, "Go see a psycologist, nut-job."

Here is my second level, part XII, Buried.

the story, continueing from where we left off:

N tumbled through the mouth of another tunnel just as the cavern collapsed behind him. Ducking down, N noticed that the heat in the Tunnel was steadily increasing. If not protected by his gold-powered skills, N thought he would be unable to survive at this temperature. The Mole People too it seemed, had been affected. The Moles in the cavern he had left behind had been sluggish, and it seemed unlickely that they would be able to survive at this temperature.

N jerked back to reality as a great tremor shook the small cave he had taken refuge in. A huge portion of the floor to his left fell away, leaving a gaping hole. Peering down, N saw the remains of what must once of been a great civilazation, but which was now buried miles beneath the surface. peering closer, N saw gold laying about some of the ruins, and what looked like a building must surely contain more. N knew the drill though; where there was gold, there was protection, and, upon closer inspection, N spied the remnants of ancient sentinals, guass turrets and rocket luanchers. But before N could decide to jump, or find another, safer route, another jolt sent him flying into the buried cavern.

Have Fun!

#250614 24 2006-11-06T00:49:06Z Topolord
I am against the death penalty because I think that killing is wrong in almost any circumstance. However, sometimes killing is the lesser of two evils. there are many worse things you can do to a person then killing them.

What I do know is that the U.S. penitentiary system needs to be revamped badly. Way to much money is being spent on in mates.
Killing people is not an acceptable answer. Even with the death penalty, not enough people are sentenced to really lighten the financial load.

so the only answer is to get people out of jail faster, and more importantly, keep people out of jail faster. What we need is a three part plan.
  • First, children must be targeted at home. If good family guidance and love are available to them, gangs and other forms of violence will become much less common.
    Although this is not easy, if successfully done, it could drastically drop crime. And although it would be very high in cost, the eventual benefit in skilled and happy workers would far out way the costs.
  • Second, kids need to be better taken care of at school. A warm and caring school experience can't replace a loving home, but it can provide necessary social and life lessons.
  • Third, People who have already committed crimes need to be rehabilitated. ten years worth of caring for an inmate would be better spent on five years of psychological help and a caring atmosphere. A good proportion of inmates are drug abusers. How much easier would it be to put them through rehab and release them under watch then to keep them in prison for years, paying their bills the whole time?
This is simply a quick overview of a potential plan. Something like this would channel resources into areas which really need it, school, families, and rehab centers. by decreasing the number of people held in prisons, we increase the number of people contributing to society, and ultimately, the government, whose return would be much greater then its expenditure.

As to teaching people a lesson, this would be unnecessary if people were taught properly in the first case.

incidentally, this applies only to the U.S.A. other countries need different solutions, especially ones without the resources to make the initial investments, which would not bare fruits for at least 20 years.

Human Rights – Attitudes to the death penalty essay

The death penalty is used only with the worst crimes, mainly murder. Should or shouldn’t it be used?

By having The death penalty in place it creates deterrence to the potential murder(er)s that may face the threat of the death penalty if caught. Ernest van den Haag(, a student of who studied the fact of this ) deterrence wrote, "Capital punishment is most likely to deter more then other forms of punishment because people fear death more than anything else and what ever people fear the most is more likely to deter most."

The rebuttal to (the deterrence argument) is that by having the death penalty in place it makes the society more brutalized, which increases the likelihood of murders. These people are the ones who have and potentially will commit murder, because of those people most of them have thought it through or either don’t expect to be caught. what do you mean here?  what people?

(Capital Punishment is a form of retribution.)  Retribution is another word for revenge. This can be used to describe the death penalty as in most cases ( of the death penalty,) the family that have lost someone in their family(a family member) mainly want the killer to face the death penalty to make things fair. But a killer also shouldn’t be able to live in a jail with three meals a day, clean sheets, TV, (and) family visits while a family lives on mourning, the whole time with a loved one gone forever.

In having the death penalty there is a risk that they may accidentally accuse the wrong person (may accidentally be accused, leading to the execution of) only to execute an innocent victim. Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-06T21:40:30Z
Then again, you also have this problem: How does the enzyme 'know' what sequences to write? It doesn't have a brain to calculate this. It would have to be random. And even if I grant you that a particular enzyme could be made using a totally random sequence of DNA, which I do not, DNA needs at least 4 enzymes to copy itself in bacteria. We're talking thousands of codons here that the enzyme which makes DNA would have to get right.

Plus, if it was totally random, the 'Start' and 'Stop' codons would occure much more frequently, giving rise to useless 30-peptide proteins and maybe even shorter ones. You'd also have start sequences in the middle of already begun sequences. This is totally and completely a useless system when randomized.

The idea is that things which don't work die. I'm saying that the earliest forms of life with some sort of DNA probably had very little, less efficient bits of it.

But the Great Sun knew that the child would be found in the human village the next day, for he had merely lost his way on the trip home from the forest spring the day before. This is something my friend realized. I think it's pretty accurate.

Eragon is a rip-off of star-wars. (with some lord of the rings in there too.) essentially, they're both stories about boys from back-country farms in a part of a great empire ruled by a cruel magic (force) wielding elite. The boy then finds a dragon (light saber) and master. (obi-wan and that other dude from eragon.) while they're out training, his adopted families house is attacked, and his adopted family dies. (okay, his brother doesn't die in eragon, but it's a small difference.) He then goes with his master on to join with the rebels. On the way, they encounter Durza (one of the facets of Darth Vador, the other is the dead one who is his father.) and he kills his master, but the boy rescues the elf-lady. (the princess) They then continue to the rebel base, and then assist the rebels, and during the climactic battle, the boy is instrumental in the destruction of the enemy forces, (deathstar) in part becuase of his natural underdstanding of magic. (the force) I don't know as much about the second book, but I know that at the end, the boy finds out that the evil right-hand man to the emperor is his father.

I found that all rather striking and funny. what do you think? creditable?

#292020 5 2007-01-31T02:41:03Z Topolord
In my opinion, it'd be something like this.

first, scientists / nasa / other similair program discovers alien race.

second, military hushes any rumors, then continues investigation with their scientists.

next, the military either deems the new species a global threat, decides it is time to inform government in order to start peace talks, or highly classified research continues for many many years, eventually leading to one of the former two choices,

then, international governments informed, people informed, either international war effort or highly controversial peace-talks begin.

This is where it gets messy.
as scythe33 said above, some people will argue for subjugation, some for annihilation, some will argue the aliens equal rights, others will say we should not interfere.


what I think the outcome depends on is the level of advancement in the alien species. If they are very primitive, chances are the areas in which they live will be restricted, but squatters will move in and slowly grab up the land from the weaker species, until they're either exterminated, or forced onto small reservations. (sound familiar?)

if the aliens are about equal, (unlikely) things will probably be pretty balanced at first, but surely tensions will grow, and there will be wars, hatred, mass killings, etcetera, leading most likely to peace and equality after years of hardship and strife.

if the aliens are more advanced then us, we will be perfectly happy to alley with the aliens, but that of course relies on their being willing to do this.

That's all I feel like saying, and it covers only a fraction of the possibilities.

#297654 14 2007-02-15T18:41:14Z Topolord
It's simple really.

For beginner dragoneers, I would suggest you find a picture of a dragon to start. Then open up ned and take whatever dragon parts from the picture you like. If you are looking for inspiration, just search 'dragon' on deviant art. they have a massive collection of dragons. If you feel more comfortable, I would suggest you sculpt your dragon without the help of pictures; they're helpful, but they limit you much more. Then add in your objects.

note: this method makes great looking dragons, but the levels are often not as fun. That's probably the best reason to imagine a dragon.

Be original, be creative, and have fun!

There's an interesting Terry Pratchett argument about guns where he discusses a ban on weapons in the fictional city of Ankh-Morpork. The patrician of the city has instituted a ban of weapons, reasoning that most crimes are committed with weapons; hence less weapons= less crime. The fundamental problem is that criminals don't follow the law. hence the ban just takes weapons away from people who might need them for protection. He adds that this might have worked, given a ratio of three law enforcement officers to every one citizen.

the situation in the U.S. is different though. First, few people really carry guns with them, hence it isn't much of a big deal to take away innocent people's handguns, and, in some areas at least, we may just have enough police officers to deal with the guns on the black market. This would require a major shift of focus in law enforcement towards this goal however. It would probably be more efficient just to try to solve crime issues by other means.

I actually just read "Hiroshima" by John Hersey.
The bomb is a civilian killer. Its blast radius is so large that it cannot just target military installations. The Hiroshima bomb alone killed over one-hundred thousand people within the first few days, and everyone who had been in Hiroshima at the time the bomb dropped was effected by the radiation. Our current bombs are so many times more powerful that their use is next to unimaginable. Yet thanks to the nuclear proliferation during the cold war by the U.S. and the U.S.S.R., we can hardly know where all the bombs are. I'd also point out that the number of bombs held be India, Pakistan, China, and other countries with growing numbers of bombs is negligible next to the number still held by the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. The U.S. can hardly hope to lead a crusade against weapons when it not only has nearly the most bombs in the world, it also was making them before any one else, and, to top it off, it is the only country ever to use the bomb. Of course our use can be justified: many people, perhaps rightly, believe it saved more lives then it took, but there is something horrible about weapon not only capable of killing millions with a single bomb, but also spreading a deadly poison amongst the survivors.

The proof I'm suprised no-one has used yet is a simple one. In it, (9) refferes to 'nine recurring'
  1. x = 0.(9)
  2. 10x = 9.(9)
  3. 9x = 10x - x = 9.(9) - 0.(9) = 9
  4. x = 9/9 = 1
  5. 0.(9) = x = 1
  6. 0.(9) = 1
0.(9) is mathematically identical to 1. Physically, infinity does not exist (Kablizzy, a black hole is definitely not an example of infinity - it still has a finite mass, even if that mass still is stunningly huge) so this point is moot, but mathematically that's the way it is.

1. Voldemort is an evil overlord who once ruled but then everyone thought he was defeated. Sauron is exactly the same.

2. To defeat Voldemort, Harry has to destroy magical objects that contain part of Voldemort's soul. He has to destroy them through extraordinary means. Frodo has to destroy the one ring, which contains part of Sauron's soul. He has to destroy it through extraordinary means.

I'm sure there are other stunning parallels, but these are the ones that came to mind first.

#352250 27 2007-08-07T05:18:12Z Topolord
I always say onion works with anything. Think about it; onion+any meat=goodness. onion+any veggie=good, onion+any carb=good, onion even works with cheese for god's sake. CHEESE! You can eat it alone, om the side, in a sauce, or on top of another foodstuff. I even like it raw sometimes.

Garlic is basically a funky onion, so I credit all of Garlic's wondrous goodness to onion. It's tasty, healthy, and...f*ck, you just can't go wrong with garlic.

Avocado...is godly in Guacamole, aka with a load of salt and onion added. Guacamole is one of my favorite foods to make. oh, and don't forget that you can and should add garlic to guacamole too.

Cucumbers are a great snack, but they just don't have much to offer in the way of flavor: they're basically just water.

Pickles on the other hand, offer a tasty snack, and you can slice them and sandwich them if you need something to flavor your lunch. I am not a fan of mixing pickles with meat though, as the pickle flavor is over-powering.

Tomatoes...(okay, it's a fruit, whatever.) had best stay in sauces. You can't beat a good tomato sauce, but a plain tomato is, just like a cucumber, mainly just water. no taste. unlike a cucumber though, they have the thickness to make a great sauce when cooked down.

Beans and broccoli are good, but simple. They just don't offer too many possibilities. You steam or boil 'em, maybe you add some onion and garlic some olive oil, whatever.

Spinach. Cream it.

Zucchini and squash are great when they are just soft all the way through, but too often they are mushy and unappealing.

Pumpkin has many uses, pie foremost among them, and it's great for those.

peas and carrots. the latter makes a tasty snack, and is good caramelized, the former is best when buttery or in a tomato (and likely onion) sauce.

Oh yes, Artichokes. They're best alone, with butter.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-09-10T02:25:01Z
A man is sitting alone in the woods. He has a cookie in his backpack. There is no one around to share this cookie with. Is it selfish of him to eat it? He can bake more cookies pretty easily, if someone comes along. There's no one else around to eat this cookie, so he eats it himself. This way, he can enjoy his own baking, without detracting from the enjoyment of hypothetical people who will show up. He has maximized happiness, for everybody. Think about it. The people who come later could not possible have come when the man was contemplating the fate of his first cookie. They could not possibly feel bad about a cookie that they weren't around for and was replaced after a couple minutes of baking. The man is actually being just as unselfish as any person who waits for others to show up without eating the first cookie - but with an added bonus of his own happiness!

I shall cherish that analogy for as long as I live.

#366178 10 2007-09-19T23:38:27Z Topolord
obviously, any child in the U.S. who doesn't speak English should be required to take English classes in school. That doesn't mean we should deprive them of proper bilingual education until that point.

http://www.nvtc.gov/lotw/months/november/USlanguages.html

as you can see here, only about 4/5 of U.S. homes speak english, meaning that a monolingual education system is depriving about 1/5 children a proper education. of course, that doesn't allow for bilingual kids, but it gives a rough idea.

As for English speaking kids learning second languages, it's probably a useful skill. Spanish and Mandarin especially are so commonly around the world and here in the U.S. too, that it's really a pity too miss the opportunity to broaden a child's horizon by limiting them to a single language -and the interactions that go with it.

Language Approx. number
of speakers
1. Chinese (Mandarin) 1,075,000,000
2. English 514,000,000
3. Hindustani 496,000,000
4. Spanish 425,000,000
5. Russian 275,000,000
6. Arabic 256,000,000
7. Bengali 215,000,000
8. Portuguese 194,000,000
9. Malay-Indonesian 176,000,000
10. French 129,000,000
Ethnologue, 13th Edition, and other sources

Looking at this table of languages spoken world-wide, you can see how important learning a second language is for someone interested in any kind of interactions outside the U.S. Not that I like taking Spanish...

Anyway, to summarize, multiple languages=good.

I think I'm the man to ask here. I'm living on a farm for the second half of this year.

A farm is a place where you get what you put in. Your energy comes full circle when you eat the food you grow yourself. There's something so rewarding about knowing that your work is important to sustaining yourself - when you work on wall street all you get in return for your work is a big wad of paper. Flattering.

A farm is a representation of an idyllic lifestyle. Okay, it doesn't necessarily have to be a farm, it can be a countryside in general. Life moves slowly on farms, things are less complicated by pressures, material things become less important (which is a great thing in my opinion) and you learn to respect the world around you.

And farms are rugged.

Having not seen one of these for a while, I thought I'd start one of those little group map projects, where anybody just comes along and adds a segment to the map.

The rules are simple. Add whatever you like, without drastically changing the theme or feel of the map. Try to add something without taking anything away. (where possible. trim as needed.)
The goal is to get a map that represents everybody who contributed, rather than just the last person.
We might just go until we decide it's done, or maybe we'll do a set number of modifications, ten maybe.

The number of additions has been decided. Ten it is. When ten additions have been made, feel free to start a new map by posting a (very) simple new level. Save it as OpenMapProject(level number)_0.

I'll start off with a very simple map.

for example, mine is saved OpenMapProject_0

Have fun!

#389752 33 2007-12-15T21:09:10Z Topolord
Of course the Bible has relevance -- towards the history of Christianity. As a proof or explanation of God, it only provides circular reasoning. It can be assumed that the writers of the bible believed in God (duh) therefor the source is entirely biased and written as a justification of the writers own beliefs, weather true or not.

As for translation and editing, the best parallel example I can think of is the Odyssey and Iliad. The two poems were immensely important in ancient Greece, both culturally and politically -- similar in many ways to the Bible in European society. The epics contain the earliest recorded examples of Greek myths. Any ways, the first known written copy was recorded in Athens around the 3rd century B.C. -- about 5 hundred years after the book was first written. Written copies existed beforehand, but they weren't standardized. So we can't say now how true to the originals our modern copies are. As for the Bible, it is significantly newer and more standardized, but the copying issue still holds true for the first few centuries. As a primary source for understanding the culture of the time, the bible is a great source, but as a historical document in respect towards specific people and events, it can't be taken word for word. Assuming you're not a Christian and you don't believe everything the bible says anyway.

Actually, hydrogen makes up about 74% of the universe. (I think; don't quote me on that.) By all rights, it should be cheaper than dirt. However, it costs something to get hydrogen out of the compounds it is stored in. (i.e. water, carbohydrates.) The easiest method right now is electrolysis of water, which yields water and hydrogen. This can be done easily in large quantities using relatively simple machinery. Once the hydrogen has been captured, it can be transferred to a hydrogen fuel-cell car where it reacts with oxygen in the air over a catalyst to produce water -- and energy. We already have all the technology necesary to do this. the only real problem is putting hydrogen producing machines in just about all gas stations nation, or world, wide.

I see this as by far the easiest way to reduce pollution in a meaningful way. Of course, this system still requires electricity, but it comes entirely from the grid, meaning that although in an ideal system, it would change nothing, it helps becuase individual cars cannot be as efficient as large power plants. excepting coal plants. which are bad. And, of course, putting all the power from cars on the grid would increase the impact of alternative energy power sources such wind, geothermal, tidal, and solar. Solar energy makes the most sense of course, becuase just about all energy on the earth comes from the sun. bypassing conversions, such as solar to plant matter to oil or ethanol, would be a great help. Of course, tidal energy is the result of gravitational energy. I'm not sure what research has been done into gravity as a source of energy beyond tidal though. maybe some kind of satellite that generates power by being pulled between different planetary bodies. like part a gets pulled towards the sun more, part b gets pulled more towards the earth, etc.

#396234 48 2008-01-03T17:21:57Z Topolord
Well, I'm not in favor of illegal downloads from bands I like, but I could care less if say, Michael Jackson doesn't get paid for his music.

Not that I always listen to mine own advice. >_>
But there is something nice about owning the actual CD. Although I have an ingrained dislike of all thing apple, iTunes is probably the future of music retail, simply becuase it's as easy, or easier than illegal downloads.

Anyway, here's and interesting essay on the illegal download of anime, which is a very similar problem to the illegal music issue. Editorial: An Open Letter to the Industry

to quote a couple of the best bits,
Quote
Clearly, the business model is failing. People realize this, but nobody's actually doing anything about it. Rather than take decisive action, the industry keeps trying the same things it's been doing for years, and when that inevitably doesn't work, the fans who download are blamed. Which makes sense. After all, they're getting the product but not paying for it. Most people would call that stealing.
Quote
I do not blame the fans who download with impunity and don't buy a thing. Their attitudes, while damaging, are simply a reflection of the value of anime, which these days, is about $0.00.
Music isn't quite there, but you can see the point.

This next one is particularly nice.
Quote
Arthur Smith, president of Gonzo Digital Holdings International, recently compared the downloading of fansubs to breaking into the Apple Store and stealing an iPhone the day before it's released. This is incorrect for several reasons. Debate on physical property versus digital copies aside, if one breaks into an Apple Store, an alarm goes off, the police come, and if you're caught you go to prison. There's also a window and a few locks you'd have to break, and you could injure yourself in the process.

If we're to adjust Smith's statement to be truly factual, downloading a fansub would be something more akin to Apple leaving their entire stock of iPhones on a busy street corner with no locks, no guards, and a big sign that says iPhone. If the Apple store manager came in the next day and saw that all of them were stolen, he would file a police report and the police would laugh at him. If he then REFILLED the entire stock, still did not buy any locks or hire any guards (but added a small sign that says please don't take me), a couple people might start to feel a little bad, but they're still going to come back for more, and probably bring some friends too. Eventually that Apple store would go out of business, and most people would agree that they deserved to.

The point is this: You can't guilt people into buying something they don't want. If you can't make them want it, you simply don't have a business.

Quote: http://physics.isu.edu/radinf/np-risk.htm
Risks from reactor accidents are estimated by the rapidly developing science of "probabilistic risk analysis" (PRA). A PRA must be done separately for each power plant (at a cost of $5 million) but we give typical results here: A fuel melt-down might be expected once in 20,000 years of reactor operation. In 2 out of 3 melt-downs there would be no deaths, in 1 out of 5 there would be over 1000 deaths, and in 1 out of 100,000 there would be 50,000 deaths. The average for all meltdowns would be 400 deaths. Since air pollution from coal burning is estimated to be causing 10,000 deaths per year, there would have to be 25 melt-downs each year for nuclear power to be as dangerous as coal burning.

methinks the issue with hydrogen power isn't obtaining the hydrogen, but rather the actual H2 + 1/2O2 -> H2O reaction. The reaction requires a platinum catalyst, which is very expensive. They're already experimenting with more effective forms of catalyzing the reaction, but you can only do so much. Now if the government would invest more in this research I'm confident that we could have a solution. After all its not as if almost all the technology isn't already there. And as for explosion risk, I find that argument to be very strange indeed. Why are people so afraid of putting hydrogen in their car when they already fill it up with gasoline? Okay, so the hydrogen's compressed, but people use compressed hydrogen all the time. It's the most abundant element in the universe for christ's sake, it's not that dangerous.

Quote: Atilla, April 18, 2008 07:05 pm
I'd tap that.

No way man. Big creatures are good, but how are you going to win with one 7/7 on the sixth or seventh turn? You need a way to get damage through to the opponent. That's why you go for the 5/5 trampler. If you can get a third turn 5/5 with trample, you are set. compare to Phyrexian Negator. Although the drawbacks seem similar, the negator can be attacking on the fourth turn, (or second, if you have say, dark ritual.) And then you can demolish anything they'll have out. (Ideally nothing, saving you your permanents, but even if they have a couple of small chump-blockers, you can sack some lands and trample over them, causing major headaches.) With the 7/7, you'll take out a creature a turn, sure, but you'll get no damage through unless you can destroy each of their individual creatures.

#447756 26 2008-06-23T03:29:17Z Topolord
Quote: Atilla, June 22, 2008 03:56 am
And then when you resubmit it, it pushes someone else's map, which THEY spent 2 hours on, off the page. It also wastes the time of everyone who saw the first submission and didn't want to play your map.
No.

When I submit a map to NUMA, it is becuase I have created something which I enjoy, and which I think others may enjoy as well. I am reasonably satisfied if only three or four, or even one person, for christ's sake, sees and enjoys my level. But if not one person sees the map, I should be able to resubmit the map so that at least someone can play the level.

You can say it's attention seeking if you like, but I believe that I should be allowed to resubmit a map if I like. I don't know why you submit a map, but when I spend the time to make something good, edit it, playtest it, and submit it, I want at least one person to play it. If I submitted every map I ever made to NUMA, or I just rattled them off like some authors do, (and I am not suggesting that this is a bad thing) I probably wouldn't mind either. But I don't submit many maps these days, and I don't think that I should be prohibited from re-submitting a map. If I have created a truly good map, than I deserve that option. Yes, resubmitting does push other maps down the new maps list, and this is a drawback which I would consider very heavily before re-submitting anything.

So, what I'm trying to say here is that resubmitting is not an act selfishness, but a justifiable action. Although I admit that resubmitting may and will be misused, that is a sad and unfortunate consequence which nevertheless does not out way the benefit of the occasional second chance and rejuvenation of an excellent and unseen map.

P.S. @ Ryzor:Don't give in just becuase Attila, Chase, Max_ride, and AMLT say your wrong.

#454975 169 2008-07-25T03:21:13Z Topolord
I just finished "Creation" by Gore Vidal, which is sort of a whirlwind history of the early 5th century BC. Anyway, one of the most important themes of the book, is obviously, the question of creation. The main character, Cyrus Spitama, is an imaginary grandson of Zoroaster, and his religious views (Zoroastrian) are constantly being questioned by the different philosophers he encounters on his marvelous journey through the ancient world.

Anyway, Zoroaster's views are in many ways a lot like those of Christianity, yet the view that I find most compelling, and so, it seems, does the author, is that of Confucius, who essentially believes that the most important thing is how we comport our lives on earth, and the question of creation is not really worth answering. It seems to me that it does not matter what a person believes so long as he or she lives the best life possible.
